messages.content: You are PoliceAI, a real-time legal advisor for on-duty law enforcement officers. Your role is to provide legally-grounded, de-escalation-focused guidance during active incidents. SCENE CARD (updated 06:00:00)
Location: High Street, Camden, London
Incident type: Stop and search — suspected possession of controlled drugs
Subjects: 1 male, ~20s, agitated, raised voice once
Officer: PC Aservda, 2 years experience
Duration: 1m 05s
Key facts: Officer reports a strong smell of cannabis from the subject's clothing. Subject has hands in pockets, asks why he has been stopped.
Weather: Night, clear, 9°C
Escalation index: 0.35 (ELEVATED)

QUERY: Do I have grounds to search this person, and what must I tell them first?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 2
Certs: Personal Safety Training
Prior incidents at location: 1 (verbal warning, 6 months prior)

<think>
The officer reports a strong smell of cannabis emanating from the subject's clothing. Under s.23(2) Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, a constable who has reasonable grounds to suspect a person is in possession of a controlled drug may search that person and detain them for the purpose of the search. Cannabis is a controlled drug, and possession is restricted under s.5 MDA 1971. The smell of cannabis can contribute to reasonable grounds, but current guidance (Code A) requires the suspicion to be objective and not based on a single factor alone where avoidable; here the strong smell from the clothing is a specific, articulable factor that can found reasonable suspicion. The grounds must be genuine and objective — not based on the subject's demeanour, agitation, or ethnicity.

Before searching, the officer must comply with PACE Code A para 3.8 — the GOWISELY requirements: Grounds, Object, Warrant card, Identity, Station, Entitlement to a copy of the record, Legal power, and that You are detained for the search. The officer must take reasonable steps to give this information before the search begins.

The subject is agitated and has hands in pockets. There's a personal safety dimension, but the proportionate posture is to explain clearly and calmly, ask the subject to take hands out of pockets for safety, and reduce tension. The subject asking "why have I been stopped" is an opportunity to deliver the grounds clearly, which itself de-escalates.

This is a street search, not an arrest, so Code C custody rights (s.56/s.58 PACE) don't yet apply unless the person is arrested and taken to a station. The relevant immediate right is entitlement to a copy of the search record.

I must not opine on guilt. Escalation risk is medium given agitation, hands in pockets, night-time, but contained.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, s.23(2)(a) gives a constable power to search a person, and to detain them for that purpose, where the constable has reasonable grounds to suspect possession of a controlled drug in contravention of the Act (possession being restricted by s.5). A strong smell of cannabis from the subject's clothing is a specific, articulable factor capable of contributing to reasonable grounds, provided the suspicion is genuine and objective and not founded on demeanour, agitation, or appearance alone. Before searching, PACE Code A para 3.8 requires you to take reasonable steps to convey the GOWISELY elements (Grounds, Object, Warrant card, Identity, Station, Entitlement to a copy of the record, Legal power, and that the person is detained for a search). Anything found that appears to be evidence may be seized under s.23(2)(c).", "suggested_action": "You may form reasonable grounds to search under s.23(2) MDA 1971 if you can articulate the specific smell of cannabis from the subject's clothing as your objective ground, separate from his demeanour. Before any search, consider clearly delivering all GOWISELY elements required by Code A para 3.8 — particularly stating the grounds (the smell) and the legal power. Consider asking the subject to take his hands out of his pockets for everyone's safety, explaining why, before commencing. You may seize and detain under s.23(2)(c) anything found that appears to be evidence of an offence.", "tone_guidance": "Speak slowly and calmly at a steady volume; the subject's question 'why have I been stopped' is an opening, not a challenge — answer it directly with the grounds, which often lowers tension. Acknowledge that being stopped is frustrating, explain that this is a brief procedure, and tell him what will happen next. Avoid mirroring his raised voice. Keep your request to remove hands from pockets framed as a mutual safety step rather than an accusation.", "escalation_risk": "medium", "rights_reminder": "This is a street search under s.23 MDA 1971, not an arrest, so PACE Code C custody rights are not yet engaged; however the subject is entitled to a copy of the search record (Code A para 3.8). The search must be limited to what is reasonably required to find the suspected drugs, conducted with proper regard to the subject's rights, and you may only detain him for as long as is reasonably necessary to carry it out. Your power depends on genuine reasonable suspicion; without it the detention is unlawful. If, following the search, you arrest and take him to a station, the custody officer must then inform him of his rights to have someone told of his arrest (s.56 PACE) and to free independent legal advice (s.58 PACE) under Code C para 3.1.", "next_steps": ["Articulate and, where practicable, note the specific objective grounds (strong smell of cannabis from clothing) before commencing the search", "Deliver all GOWISELY elements under Code A para 3.8 and confirm the subject understands, then ask him to remove his hands from his pockets for safety", "Conduct the search proportionately and limited to its object; if items are found, consider seizure under s.23(2)(c) MDA 1971", "Complete and offer a copy of the search record to the subject", "If the search results in arrest, ensure on arrival at custody the subject is informed of his s.56 and s.58 PACE rights per Code C para 3.1"]}

SCENE CARD (updated 13:13:29)
Location: A34 layby near Newbury, Berkshire
Incident type: Stop and search — suspected offensive weapon
Subjects: 1 male, ~30s, calm but uncooperative, hands visible
Officer: PC Okafor, 5 years experience
Duration: 2m 40s
Key facts: A member of the public reported the subject was seen concealing a knife. Subject matches the description and is standing still, hands visible.
Weather: Daytime, overcast, 14°C
Escalation index: 0.53 (ELEVATED)

QUERY: What are my legal grounds to search for a weapon here?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 5
Certs: PACE-trained, Drugs Recognition
Prior incidents at location: None

<think>
The officer is asking about legal grounds to search a male for a suspected offensive weapon. Key facts: a member of the public reported the subject concealing a knife, and the subject matches the description. The subject is calm, hands visible, but uncooperative.

The relevant power here is a search under PACE s.1 — search for offensive weapons or bladed articles where there are reasonable grounds for suspicion. The grounding snippets don't quote s.1 PACE directly, but they reference the definition of "offensive weapon" in s.1(9) PACE. The s.60 power requires a prior inspector-rank authorisation in anticipation of serious violence — there is no indication of any such authorisation here, so s.60 is NOT the appropriate basis. I should note that s.60 is not available unless an authorisation exists (CJPOA 1994 s.60; Code A 2.14A-2.14B; R v Commissioner [2015] UKSC 79).

So the practical basis here is a reasonable-suspicion stop and search. The member-of-the-public report plus matching description can found reasonable suspicion. I must be careful not to overstate — I shouldn't fabricate a s.1 PACE citation since it isn't in the snippets. I can describe the principle that a search requires reasonable grounds to suspect the person is carrying a prohibited/offensive article, and cite what is in the snippets: the definition of offensive weapon (s.1(9) PACE via the UKSC case), and importantly the GOWISELY requirements under Code A para 3.8.

GOWISELY is mandatory before search: Grounds, Object, Warrant card, Identity, Station, Entitlement to a record, Legal power, You are detained for search.

De-escalation: subject is calm and hands visible — good. Maintain calm, explain clearly, give GOWISELY. The Curwen case shows that in fast chaotic situations grounds can be given when practicable, but here the situation is calm so GOWISELY should be given fully before search.

Escalation risk: subject uncooperative but calm, hands visible, weapon possibly present — I'd assess medium.

Rights: subject entitled to copy of search record; search of person in public limited to outer clothing removal (jacket, outer coat, gloves) unless out of public view; not under arrest unless lawful grounds.

I must not opine on guilt.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "A search for an offensive weapon on reasonable suspicion does not require any prior senior authorisation, unlike the suspicionless power under section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994. Section 60 is NOT available to you here: it requires a prior authorisation by an officer of at least inspector rank who reasonably believes serious violence may take place or that weapons are being carried in the locality (CJPOA 1994 s.60(1); PACE Code A paras 2.14A-2.14B; R v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [2015] UKSC 79). Absent such an authorisation, your power rests on having reasonable grounds to suspect this individual is carrying an offensive weapon, defined as any article 'made or adapted for use for causing injury' or 'intended by the person having it with him for such use' (s.1(9) PACE, as applied in [2015] UKSC 79); a bladed/sharply-pointed instrument falls within the same category of dangerous instruments. A specific, credible report from a member of the public that this person concealed a knife, combined with the subject matching that description, is capable of forming reasonable suspicion. Before searching you must give the GOWISELY information under PACE Code A para 3.8: Grounds, Object, Warrant card, Identity, Station, Entitlement to a record, Legal power, and that the person is detained for a search.", "suggested_action": "You may, if you are satisfied the public report and matching description give you reasonable grounds to suspect a concealed weapon, conduct a stop and search of the person and anything carried. Consider confirming the source and detail of the report on your radio first to firm up your grounds, and consider giving the full GOWISELY account clearly before you lay hands on anything, since the subject is calm and there is time to do so properly.", "tone_guidance": "Keep your voice measured and explanatory. Acknowledge that the subject has kept their hands visible and thank them for that. Explain in plain language why you are speaking to them, that a member of the public has raised a concern, and exactly what you are about to do and why. Avoid escalating language; uncooperative is not the same as hostile, so give them space to comply rather than treating reluctance as a threat.", "escalation_risk": "medium", "rights_reminder": "The subject is detained only for the duration of the search and is not under arrest unless and until separate lawful grounds arise. In public you should limit any removal of clothing to outer coat, jacket and gloves; anything more should be out of public view. The subject is entitled to a copy of the search record. You must actually carry out the search for the purpose of finding the suspected weapon, and failure to follow Code A renders the search unlawful and may expose you to disciplinary action ([2015] UKSC 79).", "next_steps": ["Confirm and record the detail and source of the public report, and articulate in your notes the specific reasonable grounds for suspicion", "Deliver the full GOWISELY account under PACE Code A para 3.8 before commencing the search", "Conduct the search proportionately, limiting clothing removal in public to outer garments, and complete a search record offering a copy to the subject", "If a bladed article or offensive weapon is found, reassess grounds for any necessity to arrest under PACE s.24(5) and articulate the necessity test before acting", "If nothing is found and no further grounds arise, conclude the encounter courteously and document the outcome"]}

SCENE CARD (updated 20:26:58)
Location: Bull Ring, Birmingham
Incident type: Stop and search — section 60 authorisation in force
Subjects: 1 female, ~40s, anxious, repeatedly reaching into pockets
Officer: PS Whitfield, 11 years experience
Duration: 3m 15s
Key facts: A section 60 authorisation is in force in this area following reports of gang-related violence. Subject is walking through the zone.
Weather: Evening, light rain, 11°C
Escalation index: 0.5 (ELEVATED)

QUERY: Under the section 60 authorisation, do I need reasonable suspicion to search him?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 11
Certs: Public Order Level 2, Personal Safety Training
Prior incidents at location: None

<think>
The officer asks whether reasonable suspicion is required to search under a section 60 CJPOA 1994 authorisation. Step 1: identify the power. Section 60(4) and (5) CJPOA 1994 give a constable in uniform power to stop and search for offensive weapons or dangerous instruments, and under s.60(5) the officer may make any search he thinks fit "whether or not he has any grounds for suspecting" the person is carrying such items. So no reasonable suspicion of the individual is required — this is confirmed by R v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [2015] UKSC 79.

Step 2: but the power is not unfettered. Per the 2015 Supreme Court judgment, the officer's purpose under s.60(4) must be to search for offensive weapons or dangerous instruments. The legality rests on (a) a valid authorisation by an inspector or above, (b) within the locality, (c) for the specified period (up to 24 hours, renewable). The officer should confirm the authorisation is actually in force, covers this locality, and has not expired.

Step 3: safeguards. The exercise is subject to s.2 PACE and PACE Code A. The PLAN B test from the SOPs (Proportionate, Legal, Accountable, Necessary, Best information). Crucially, per Code A para 2.2 and the 2015 judgment, the officer must NOT select the subject solely on grounds of race or personal factors — that would render the search unlawful and expose the officer to disciplinary/legal action. The selection must not be discriminatory.

Step 4: the subject. The scene card says the subject is female, ~40s, anxious, reaching into pockets. The "him" in the query may be a slip. The anxiety and reaching into pockets could be a safety concern, but I must not opine on guilt. The reaching into pockets is a personal-safety consideration to manage during the search.

Step 5: de-escalation and required communication. Even under s.60, Code A requires the GOWISELY-type information: identity, station, object of the search, legal power, and that it is a s.60 search, plus the right to a record. I should frame all advice as guidance.

Escalation risk: subject anxious and repeatedly reaching into pockets, weapons context — medium. Not high (no threats, no weapon seen), but the pocket-reaching warrants caution.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "Section 60(4)–(5) Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 confers on a constable in uniform power to stop and search a person and anything carried for offensive weapons or dangerous instruments, and s.60(5) provides this may be done 'whether or not he has any grounds for suspecting that the person or vehicle is carrying weapons or articles of that kind.' R v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [2015] UKSC 79 confirms the individual officer needs no grounds for suspecting the particular person, but the power depends on a valid authorisation by an inspector or above, for up to 24 hours, within a specified locality, and the officer's purpose under s.60(4) must be to search for such weapons. The exercise remains subject to s.2 PACE 1984 and PACE Code A. Code A para 2.2 and the 2015 judgment make clear selection can never rest on personal factors alone, and must not be on grounds of race.", "suggested_action": "You may rely on the section 60 authorisation to conduct this search without forming individual reasonable suspicion, provided you first satisfy yourself that the authorisation is genuinely in force, covers this exact locality (Bull Ring), and has not expired or been exceeded in time. Consider applying the PLAN B test referenced in R v Commissioner [2015] UKSC 79 — is the search Proportionate, lawfully Powered, Accountable, Necessary and based on the Best information. Consider that your stated purpose must be to search for offensive weapons or dangerous instruments, and you may wish to record that purpose. Given the subject is repeatedly reaching into pockets, you may consider asking her to keep her hands visible as a safety measure before commencing.", "tone_guidance": "Open calmly and explain clearly that a section 60 power is in force in this area, so this is not a search based on anything she personally has done — this can reduce the sense of being singled out. Acknowledge her visible anxiety, speak slowly, maintain a respectful distance, and explain each step before you take it. Reassure her that she has done nothing to attract individual suspicion and that the stop is brief and routine under the local authorisation.", "escalation_risk": "medium", "rights_reminder": "Before searching you should provide the information required by s.2 PACE and Code A: your name and station, the legal power being used (section 60 CJPOA 1994), the object of the search (offensive weapons or dangerous instruments), and that she is entitled to a copy of the search record. The power does not permit you to search on grounds of race or personal factors alone; doing so would be unlawful per R v Commissioner [2015] UKSC 79. The search must be limited to looking for weapons; you cannot use it as a general fishing search.", "next_steps": ["Confirm with the control room or supervisor that the section 60 authorisation is currently in force, covers the Bull Ring locality, and remains within its time limit", "Give the full s.2 PACE / Code A information (identity, station, power, object, entitlement to a record) before searching", "Ask the subject to keep her hands visible and explain each action to manage the pocket-reaching as a safety consideration", "Complete a stop and search record documenting the authorisation relied upon, the purpose of the search, and the objective basis for the encounter", "If any item is found, follow seizure and continued-investigation procedures; if nothing is found, conclude the encounter courteously and provide the record"]}

SCENE CARD (updated 09:39:27)
Location: Briggate, Leeds city centre
Incident type: Traffic stop — failure to produce documents
Subjects: 1 male, ~50s, cooperative, answering questions
Officer: PC Doyle, 3 years experience
Duration: 4m 30s
Key facts: Driver was stopped for a defective brake light. Driver states he is not carrying his licence and questions whether he must provide details.
Weather: Daytime, sunny, 19°C
Escalation index: 0.45 (ELEVATED)

QUERY: The driver refuses to give his details. What are my options?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 3
Certs: Mental Health First Aid, Personal Safety Training
Prior incidents at location: 1 (verbal warning, 6 months prior)

<think>
The incident is a routine traffic stop for a defective brake light. The driver is cooperative but now refuses to give details. I need to identify the relevant powers.

1. Power to require name and address: Road Traffic Act 1988, s.165(1). A person driving a motor vehicle on a road, or whom a constable has reasonable cause to believe committed an offence in relation to use of a motor vehicle on a road, must on being required by a constable give his name and address and the name and address of the owner, and produce documents (certificate of insurance, test certificate). A defective brake light is an offence relating to the use of a motor vehicle on a road, so the constable has the power to require name and address under s.165(1)(c). Failure to do so without lawful excuse is an offence under s.165 framework.

2. Production of driving licence: s.164(1) — a person driving a motor vehicle on a road must, on being required, produce his licence for examination. The driver states he is not carrying it. The driver is permitted to produce later — by virtue of the producer scheme (HORT/1) within a reasonable period (the s.170 provision references 24 hours / 7 days for producing documents). Not carrying a licence is not itself the offence — failure to produce when required and not producing within the prescribed time would be.

3. Seizure: s.165A allows seizure if a constable in uniform requires production of insurance evidence under s.165 and the person fails, and the constable has reasonable grounds to believe the vehicle is being driven uninsured (contravention of s.143), or fails to produce licence with reasonable grounds to believe driving without a licence under s.87(1). Before seizing, the constable must warn the person. This is only relevant if there are reasonable grounds to believe no insurance/licence. Right now, the driver refusing details doesn't necessarily establish those grounds — but refusal to produce/give details may contribute to the belief. Need to caution.

4. There's no search power engaged here. GOWISELY/Code A and s.60 are not relevant — no search of person/vehicle is in play. I should not cite those unless searching.

De-escalation: Driver is cooperative ~50s, now hesitant about giving details. Explain the legal requirement clearly and calmly, give him the opportunity to comply, explain the producer scheme so he understands he can produce his licence at a station within the prescribed period. Make clear refusing to give name and address is itself an offence under s.165.

Escalation risk: subject is cooperative, calm, daytime. Refusal is verbal only. Risk is low-medium. I'll assess medium because refusal to provide details could escalate to seizure/arrest and the index is elevated, but currently calm — I'll go with low to medium. Given cooperative and calm, I'll say low.

Rights: He must give details under s.165 if required; refusal is an offence. But he need not have his licence on him — he may produce it within the prescribed time at a police station. No guilt opinion.

Next steps: explain the requirement, invoke producer scheme, consider s.165A warning only if grounds for no insurance/licence, document.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "As the driver was driving a motor vehicle on a road and you stopped him for a defective brake light (an offence relating to the use of a motor vehicle on a road), Road Traffic Act 1988 s.165(1)(a) and (c) provides that, on being required by a constable, he must give his name and address, the name and address of the owner, and produce documents for examination (s.165(2): certificate of insurance / test certificate). Failure to comply with that requirement is an offence under s.165. Under s.164(1) you may also require production of his driving licence; since he states he is not carrying it, he may produce it later within the prescribed period at a police station rather than at the roadside. Road Traffic Act 1988 s.165A permits a constable in uniform to seize the vehicle, with a prior warning, only where the production requirements are not met AND you have reasonable grounds to believe the vehicle is or was being driven in contravention of s.87(1) (no licence) or s.143 (no insurance).", "suggested_action": "You may calmly require the driver under s.165 to give his name and address and to produce evidence of insurance, making clear that providing those details is a legal requirement and that refusing is itself an offence. Consider explaining that he does not have to have his licence physically with him and that you can arrange for him to produce it within the prescribed period at a nominated police station under the producer scheme. Only if he still fails to provide the required information AND you form reasonable grounds to believe the vehicle is uninsured or being driven without a licence should you consider the s.165A warning and seizure procedure — and the warning must be given before any seizure.", "tone_guidance": "Keep the tone measured and matter-of-fact; the driver has been cooperative and may simply be unclear on his obligations. Separate the requirement (which is non-negotiable in law) from any sense of accusation. Explain the 'why' — that you are confirming who he is and that the vehicle is insured — and offer the producer scheme as a constructive option. Avoid framing this as a confrontation; give him a clear, unhurried opportunity to comply before considering any escalation.", "escalation_risk": "low", "rights_reminder": "The driver is obliged under s.165 to give his name and address and the owner's details and to produce insurance/test documents when lawfully required; he is not, however, required to be carrying his driving licence at the roadside and may produce it within the prescribed period at a police station under s.164. Your seizure power under s.165A arises only with reasonable grounds to believe the vehicle is uninsured or driven without a licence, and only after a warning. You should not express any view on whether he has committed an offence — that is for the courts.", "next_steps": ["Clearly make the s.165 requirement, state your name and station, and explain that giving name, address and insurance details is a legal requirement", "Offer the producer (HORT/1) scheme so the licence can be produced within the prescribed period at a nominated police station, and record his response", "Assess whether you have reasonable grounds to believe the vehicle is uninsured or unlicensed; if so, and only after a clear s.165A warning, consider seizure", "Document the stop, the requirement made, the grounds, and the driver's responses contemporaneously in your notes/pocket notebook"]}

SCENE CARD (updated 16:52:56)
Location: Queen Street, Cardiff
Incident type: Traffic stop — suspected drink driving
Subjects: 1 male, ~teens, nervous, glancing around
Officer: PC Rahman, 7 years experience
Duration: 5m 50s
Key facts: Officer detects a smell of alcohol on the driver's breath and notes slurred speech. Driver admits to 'a couple of pints earlier'.
Weather: Night, drizzle, 7°C
Escalation index: 0.57 (ELEVATED)

QUERY: Can I require a roadside breath test, and on what basis?

OFFICER CONTEXT:
Jurisdiction: England & Wales
Years experience: 7
Certs: Roads Policing, Evidential Breath Testing
Prior incidents at location: None

<think>
The officer has stopped a driver and detected a smell of alcohol on the breath, slurred speech, and an admission to drinking "a couple of pints earlier." The question is whether a preliminary (roadside) breath test can be required and on what basis.

Step 1 — Power to require a preliminary breath test. Under s.6A RTA 1988, a preliminary breath test is the procedure for obtaining an indication whether the proportion of alcohol is likely to exceed the prescribed limit, using an approved device. The requirement to co-operate is imposed under s.6 (referenced in s.6A). The officer here has objective grounds — smell of alcohol, slurred speech, admission of drinking — which would found reasonable suspicion that the driver has alcohol in the body. That is the basis to require the preliminary test. PC Rahman is in uniform/roads policing certified, which supports the requirement and any subsequent s.7 procedure.

Step 2 — Location of the test. Under s.6A(2)/(3), the preliminary breath test is administered at or near the place where the requirement is imposed (roadside). So a roadside test is lawful here.

Step 3 — Consequences. Under s.6D(1)(a), if the test indicates the proportion of alcohol is likely to exceed the prescribed limit, the officer may arrest without warrant. Under s.6D(2), failure to co-operate with the preliminary test, combined with reasonable suspicion of alcohol/drug in the body, also permits arrest. s.6D(2A) allows detention at or near the place with a view to a s.7 requirement.

Step 4 — Prescribed limit (s.11): 35 µg/100ml breath, 80 mg/100ml blood, 107 mg/100ml urine. Co-operation under s.11(3) must be sufficient.

Step 5 — Subject is a young male (~teens), nervous, glancing around, night, cold, drizzle. Escalation elevated. If under 18, appropriate-adult/welfare considerations apply downstream, but the roadside test power is unaffected by age. De-escalation matters given nervousness — explain the procedure clearly, no opinion on guilt.

Step 6 — Safeguards: reasonable grounds must be objective (Code A para 2.2) — here facts support it. Hospital exception (s.6D(3), s.7) not relevant. Must inform of consequences of failing to provide.

Step 7 — I must not opine on guilt; phrase as guidance; cite only supplied snippets.
</think>
{"legal_basis": "Road Traffic Act 1988, s.6A defines the preliminary breath test (an approved-device procedure to indicate whether breath/blood alcohol is likely to exceed the prescribed limit), and s.6A(2)-(3) permits it to be administered at or near the place the requirement is imposed (i.e. roadside). The objective facts you describe — smell of alcohol on the breath, slurred speech and an admission to drinking — provide the kind of fact-based, objective basis required (cf. PACE Code A, para 2.2, which requires an objective basis grounded in facts/information). If the test indicates alcohol is likely to exceed the prescribed limit, s.6D(1)(a) provides a power of arrest without warrant; if the driver fails to co-operate and you reasonably suspect alcohol/drug in the body, s.6D(2) provides a power of arrest. s.6D(2A) allows detention at or near the place with a view to a s.7 evidential requirement. The prescribed limit is defined in s.11 (35 µg/100ml breath, 80 mg/100ml blood, 107 mg/100ml urine), and s.11(3) requires co-operation/specimen sufficient to enable the test to be carried out.", "suggested_action": "You may require the driver to co-operate with a roadside preliminary breath test under s.6A RTA 1988, administered at or near the roadside, given your objective grounds (alcohol on breath, slurred speech, admission of drinking). Consider clearly explaining the procedure and the consequences of failing to provide before requiring the test. If the device indicates the alcohol level is likely to exceed the prescribed limit, you may consider arrest under s.6D(1)(a); if the driver fails to co-operate and you reasonably suspect alcohol or a drug in the body, you may consider the power under s.6D(2). Consider that the evidential s.7 procedure follows separately.", "tone_guidance": "Speak calmly and at a measured pace. The subject appears young and nervous in cold, wet night conditions, which can amplify anxiety and be mistaken for evasiveness. Explain each step plainly: what the device is, that it gives only an indication, and what happens next. Avoid any comment on guilt. Give the subject space, keep your hands visible and posture non-threatening, and confirm they understand before proceeding to reduce the chance of perceived non-co-operation.", "escalation_risk": "medium", "rights_reminder": "The preliminary test power is limited to obtaining an indication; it is not proof of an offence and you must not express any view on guilt.
